thread.title: Apple: Expectations Meet Reality - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Rohit Chhatwal
title: Apple: Expectations Meet Reality - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Whenever a strong bearish thesis for Apple ( AAPL ) is published, there's a lot of unfavorable response from a large section of commenters and investors. In one of my recent articles, Apple products will be a lot cheaper , I received close to 400 comments and over 90% were highly critical of the bearish viewpoint. Similar negative sentiment is seen on almost all bearish articles about Apple. All my articles are based on strong quantitative metrics, however, few (if any) comments are backed by any kind of data. I think there's a misalignment of expectations about Apple’s future returns. We should look closely at what is the probable range of returns for long-term investors.
Prudent expectations It is certainly fine to invest on the basis of conviction. This is one of the strongest factors which an investor can count on. However, it is also important to look at hard numbers. Investors also should consider the possible range of returns which a stock can deliver. This helps in having correct expectations from the investment and also prevents making decisions based on short-term results.
Although I'm highly bearish about future returns potential of Apple, we should also look at the returns suggested by highly bullish analysts to get a good sense of future direction for the stock. All Apple investors should read the recent article published by Dividend Sensei (NYSE: DS ), 6 reasons why Apple could keep crushing the market over the next decade . It's a strong buy thesis from one of the top contributors on Seeking Alpha.
DS has covered almost all possible points about the current state of Apple and has used numerous quantitative points to justify his views. It's a very rigorous analysis and better than any other resource one can find on open platforms. I do not agree with the risk assessment and growth potential of Apple mentioned by DS, but there are still important points one must consider.
The most significant point within the article is the return potential of Apple. DS has a strong buy rating for Apple which means the returns mentioned by him would be in the upper range of a probable scenario.
Fig: Returns potential of Apple calculated by Dividend Sensei. Source: Dividend Sensei
Detailed calculation of the potential returns can be seen in the article. The middle point of DS’s 10-year potential annual total returns for Apple comes at 13.1%, which would be 5 percentage points higher than the S&P 500. The major reasons for a strong bullish thesis from DS is based on: High FCF, capital returns, Services growth, dividend growth potential and flat unit sales in iPhone segment.
On the other hand, I have a strong bearish viewpoint for Apple. This is based on: commoditization of iPhone segment, falling margin, tapering off in Services growth, difficulty in growing already large revenue base and many more. These points have been covered in my previous articles which can be found here and here . The above headwinds should limit the growth potential of Apple’s stock. My view is that it will deliver low single digit total returns over the next 10 years. This is probably in the lowest possible range for Apple’s stock.
Nobody has a crystal ball to exactly predict future returns, however, we can look at the returns potential in a strong buy and strong sell case and see the possible range. This should help in forming more prudent expectations.
We can look at the returns based on 3% (bearish case), 8.1% (S&P 500) and 13.1% (bullish case) returns scenario.
Fig: $10,000 investment in Apple at different annualized return scenario.
Hence, a $10,000 investment in Apple will convert to $13,439 in a strong bearish scenario or $34,247 in a strong bullish scenario in the next 10 years. A $10,000 S&P 500 index investment would be $20,157 in 10 years.
I think there's 95% probability that the investment in Apple at the current price point will end up between the two extreme cases shown above in 10 years. Obviously, I have a strong tilt toward the lower end of this returns scenario.
Apple showed massive gains in the middle of last decade. The stock price increased from $2.5 in 2004 to close to $100 by 2012. This 4000% jump was possible because of the success of iPhone and low revenue base in 2004. Apple is a completely different company now with a market cap which is close to 5% of U.S. GDP. Unless Apple comes up with a cure for cancer it is difficult to see how it can show higher returns than 13.1% CAGR.
Price, Price, Price A major part of my bearish viewpoint is based on current pricing of Apple stock. Apple is trading at a PE ratio which is at the highest level in this decade.
The future growth trend within iPhone segment is much more subdued than it was in the early part of this decade. Although Services growth is often cited as a future growth engine for Apple, it still made $30 billion in revenue compared to $141 billion of sales in the iPhone segment in 2017. This means Services revenue is only 22% of iPhone revenue.
Apple has a number of tailwinds in 2017 and 2018 from outside factors. These include a weaker dollar, tax benefits and lower repatriation rate which have helped the company to increase its capital return program and boast better revenue growth in dollar terms. Over a longer period of 10 years or more, these short-term tailwinds will not matter as much as product innovation.
Even though the iPhone X came very short of earlier expectations, there has not been a correction in the earlier bull run in Apple’s stock. This reduces the upside potential at the current price and lowers the returns for longer-term investors.
Investor Takeaway It is very important to have reasonable expectations from Apple’s stock at this stage of the company. In a strong bearish scenario the long-term returns will be closer to 3% annualized and in a strong bullish scenario the long-term returns will be at most 13.1% annualized. It is statistically impossible for the stock to show returns anywhere close to what it delivered in second half of last decade.
The headwinds for the company are very strong. A higher current valuation further reduces the returns potential of the stock. Investors should either wait for some strong correction in the stock or look for other options to gain better returns than the S&P 500 index.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
